Banquetings
băŋ´kwět-īŋz
n. pl. (drinking-parties; carousals, in the KJV's older sense)
From French banquet, a feast. Peter's Greek is potos, from pino, to drink — a drinking bout, not a dinner. The KJV word has softened since 1611; the thing Peter names has not.

Biblical Definition

Peter tells a scattered church that the account is closed on what they used to be: “For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries” (1 Peter 4:3). The list ends where it does on purpose. Drinking-parties and idolatries sit in one sentence because in the ancient city they were one occasion, and because appetite indulged past its bound is already worship of something. The cost of leaving is immediate: “Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you” (1 Peter 4:4). Our Lord names the same danger as a matter of watchfulness rather than reputation: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares” (Luke 21:34). Amos had seen it in Israel's own houses: “That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall” (Amos 6:4). Scripture blesses the feast — Christ made wine at one. What it forbids is the feast that has no end and no Host.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives banqueting as feasting, and banquet as a rich entertainment; the older English carried the further sense of a drinking-bout, which is Peter's meaning.

expand to see more

BANQUETING, ppr. Feasting; delicious fare; rich entertainment.

BANQUET, n. A feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink.

SURFEITING, n. The act of feeding to excess; oppression from excessive eating and drinking.

REVEL, v.i. To feast with loose and clamorous merriment; to carouse; to act the part of a bacchanalian.

RIOT, n. Tumult; uproar; excessive and expensive feasting; luxury.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 4:3 — "For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:"

1 Peter 4:4 — "Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:"

Luke 21:34 — "And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares."

Amos 6:4 — "That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;"

Modern Corruption

Because the English word has drifted toward the harmless dinner, a plain apostolic prohibition is read as a warning against enjoying food.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift here is linguistic rather than ideological, and it runs in both directions. A reader who takes banquetings in its modern sense hears Peter forbidding hospitality, which Scripture everywhere commands; a reader who knows the word has softened may conclude the whole list is antique. Peter's potos is a drinking bout, and the sin is the indulgence, not the table. The principle to recover is that Scripture is generous about feasts and exact about their bounds.

Luke 21:34 gives the bound in a word: overcharged. A heart can be weighed down by surfeiting, by drunkenness, and — in the same clause, at the same weight — by the cares of this life. That last item is the one a sober congregation will miss. The man who would never be found at a carousal may be just as unfit to meet that day because his heart is loaded with his business. Peter's list and Christ's warning close the same door from two sides.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek potos (G4224), a drinking-bout; komos (G2970), revelling, carousal; kraipale (G2897), surfeiting.

expand to see more

Greek potos (G4224) — a drinking, carousal; only at 1 Peter 4:3, rendered banquetings.

Greek komos (G2970) — revelling; the procession of the drunken, Romans 13:13 and Galatians 5:21.

Greek kraipale (G2897) — the giddiness of over-indulgence; Luke 21:34, surfeiting.

Greek asotia (G810) — riot, unsavedness; the excess of 1 Peter 4:4 and Ephesians 5:18.

Greek oinophlugia (G3632) — excess of wine; literally a bubbling over with wine.

Usage

"“The time past of our life may suffice” — the account is closed, not reopened."

"“They think it strange that ye run not with them” — the cost of leaving."

"“Overcharged with…cares of this life” — the sober man's version of the same weight."
